newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria lev hits new record low amid uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria lev hits new record low amid uncertainty.

text.p: The Bulgarian lev hit a new record low of 600 to the dollar on Friday as investors stocked up on dollars in the face of political and economic uncertainty.
It later closed between 590-605 per dollar, down from 575-585 in the morning and 507-510 at Monday's close.
"I see 600 levs as the support level for Monday and 1,000 levs will become the average exchange rate in the next few weeks," said one resident bank dealer.
The main dollar buyers so far after the holiday recess are small firms coverting their lev earnings into dollars to avoid losses from further lev devaluation, the dealer added.
The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) was not seen selling dollars to halt the lev slide during the first trading day of 1997 for the local interbank market, dealers said.
BNB officials were not available for comment. Local markets were closed from Tuesday through Thursday for the New Year.

Bulgaria's ruling Socialists are expected to form a new cabinet by mid-January after Prime Minister Zhan Videnov resigned two weeks ago, saying he lacked the support he needed from the party and the country to continue as prime minister and party leader.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said last month it was prepared to negotiate the introduction of a tough monetary regime, called a currency board, once the political situation had become clearer.

Two IMF technical missions visited Sofia in December to prepare legal changes needed for the operation of the currency board, help draft the 1997 budget, and advise on restructuring the central bank to operate under a currency board system.
The lev has collapsed from 70 to the dollar in January 1996 to 600 on Friday.
Central bank possibilities for intervention on the domestic forex market remained limited as its foreign exchange reserves melted to $525 million at end-November from $1.3 billion a year ago.

The central bank governor said recently that foreign debt payments remained a priority. Bulgaria said it will pay $130 million coupon on Brady bonds due on January 28. The bonds were issued in 1994 to restructure an $8.1 billion commercial debt.

Dealers said the situation may become even worse as it was not yet certain whether the government would be able to cover paymets of domestic government securities of around 50 billion levs also due in January.
"The lev's weakening is inevitable. Once fuel importers reappear on the market they will push the lev lower," another commercial bank dealer said.
The IMF said last month that under a currency board system, where the amount of levs in circulation must be matched by foreign exchange reserves, the lev should be fixed at the current market rate.

"If the lev is fixed higher than its market value, Bulgarian firms will be less compatible; if it is fixed lower than its value inflation will subside more slowly," Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov told journalists recently.
The draft budget for next year is assumed at a lev/dollar rate of 500.
